name: Science
description: Physics, chemistry, biology, astronomy, earth science and the human body.
question: {prompt}

cards.prompt: What is the chemical symbol for gold?
cards.fact: Au comes from aurum, the Latin word for gold.

cards.prompt: What is the chemical symbol for iron?
cards.fact: Fe comes from ferrum, Latin for iron.

cards.prompt: What is the chemical formula for table salt?
cards.fact: Table salt is sodium chloride: one sodium atom for every chlorine atom.

cards.prompt: What is the lightest chemical element?
cards.fact: Hydrogen is also the most abundant element in the universe.

cards.prompt: What is the atomic number of carbon?
cards.fact: Every carbon atom has 6 protons; all known life is built around carbon.

cards.prompt: What is the pH of pure water at 25 °C?
cards.fact: A pH of 7 is neutral; lower is acidic and higher is basic.

cards.prompt: What is the hardest natural mineral?
cards.fact: Diamond is pure carbon and tops the Mohs hardness scale at 10.

cards.prompt: Which metal is liquid at room temperature and was used in old thermometers?
cards.fact: Mercury freezes at about −39 °C, far colder than room temperature.

cards.prompt: What is it called when a liquid turns into a gas at its surface, like a puddle drying up?
cards.fact: Evaporation cools things down, which is why sweating keeps you cool.

cards.prompt: Roughly how fast does light travel in a vacuum, in kilometers per second?
cards.fact: At about 299,792 km/s, light could circle Earth about 7.5 times in one second.

cards.prompt: What force keeps the planets in orbit around the Sun?
cards.fact: Gravity also keeps the Moon in orbit around Earth.

cards.prompt: What is the SI unit of electrical resistance?
cards.fact: It is named after German physicist Georg Ohm.

cards.prompt: What is the SI unit of force?
cards.fact: One newton is roughly the weight of a small apple.

cards.prompt: Which subatomic particle has a negative electric charge?
cards.fact: J. J. Thomson discovered the electron in 1897.

cards.prompt: At sea level, at what temperature in °C does water boil?
cards.fact: High up a mountain water boils at a lower temperature, because air pressure is lower.

cards.prompt: What is absolute zero on the Celsius scale?
cards.fact: Absolute zero, 0 kelvin, is the coldest possible temperature.

cards.prompt: Who published the theory of general relativity in 1915?
cards.fact: General relativity describes gravity as the bending of space and time by mass.

cards.prompt: Which scientist formulated the three laws of motion and the law of universal gravitation?
cards.fact: Newton set out his laws in the Principia, published in 1687.

cards.prompt: Which planet is known as the Red Planet?
cards.fact: Mars looks red because its surface is rich in iron oxide, basically rust.

cards.prompt: What is the largest planet in our Solar System?
cards.fact: More than 1,300 Earths could fit inside Jupiter.

cards.prompt: Which planet is closest to the Sun?
cards.fact: A year on Mercury lasts just 88 Earth days.

cards.prompt: Which is the hottest planet in our Solar System?
cards.fact: Venus's thick carbon dioxide atmosphere traps heat, making it hotter than Mercury.

cards.prompt: Which planet has the largest and most spectacular ring system?
cards.fact: Saturn's rings are made mostly of chunks of water ice.

cards.prompt: Which planet spins on its side, with an axial tilt of about 98°?
cards.fact: Uranus was the first planet discovered with a telescope, by William Herschel in 1781.

cards.prompt: How many planets are in our Solar System?
cards.fact: Pluto was reclassified as a dwarf planet in 2006.

cards.prompt: What is the closest star to Earth?
cards.fact: The next closest, Proxima Centauri, is about 4.2 light-years away.

cards.prompt: Roughly how long does sunlight take to reach Earth?
cards.fact: Sunlight takes about 8 minutes 20 seconds to cross 150 million km.

cards.prompt: What is the name of the galaxy we live in?
cards.fact: The Milky Way contains hundreds of billions of stars.

cards.prompt: Which element makes up most of the Sun's mass?
cards.fact: About three-quarters of the Sun is hydrogen, which it fuses into helium.

cards.prompt: Approximately how old is the universe?
cards.fact: The estimate comes largely from measurements of the cosmic microwave background.

cards.prompt: What mainly causes the ocean tides on Earth?
cards.fact: The Sun adds a smaller tidal pull, a bit under half as strong as the Moon's.

cards.prompt: What is the most abundant gas in Earth's atmosphere?
cards.fact: Nitrogen makes up about 78% of the air; oxygen is about 21%.

cards.prompt: What type of rock forms when magma or lava cools and hardens?
cards.fact: "Igneous" comes from ignis, Latin for fire; granite and basalt are examples.

cards.prompt: What was the supercontinent that existed about 250 million years ago?
cards.fact: Pangaea means "all the Earth" in Greek.

cards.prompt: Which instrument records earthquakes?
cards.fact: "Seismos" is Greek for shaking or earthquake.

cards.prompt: Which layer of the atmosphere contains the ozone layer?
cards.fact: The ozone layer absorbs most of the Sun's harmful ultraviolet radiation.

cards.prompt: What is the name of Earth's outermost solid layer?
cards.fact: The crust is thinnest under the oceans, often only 5–10 km thick.

cards.prompt: What is the most abundant element in Earth's crust by mass?
cards.fact: Oxygen makes up about 46% of the crust, mostly locked in silicate minerals.

cards.prompt: Approximately how old is the Earth?
cards.fact: Earth's age is pinned down by radiometric dating of meteorites and ancient rocks.

cards.prompt: Which gas do plants take in from the air for photosynthesis?
cards.fact: Plants release oxygen as a by-product of photosynthesis.

cards.prompt: What pigment makes plants green?
cards.fact: Chlorophyll absorbs red and blue light and reflects green.

cards.prompt: Which part of a cell is known as its "powerhouse"?
cards.fact: Mitochondria have their own DNA, separate from the cell nucleus.

cards.prompt: What is the smallest unit of life?
cards.fact: Robert Hooke coined the word "cell" in 1665 after viewing cork under a microscope.

cards.prompt: What do bees collect from flowers to make honey?
cards.fact: A single honeybee makes only about a twelfth of a teaspoon of honey in its life.

cards.prompt: What is the heaviest animal known to have ever lived?
cards.fact: Blue whales can reach about 30 m long and outweigh even the biggest known dinosaurs.

cards.prompt: What kind of animal is a Komodo dragon?
cards.fact: Komodo dragons are the largest living lizards, reaching up to about 3 m.

cards.prompt: What is the scientific study of fungi called?
cards.fact: Fungi are more closely related to animals than to plants.

cards.prompt: How many bones are in the adult human body?
cards.fact: Babies are born with around 300 bones, many of which fuse as they grow.

cards.prompt: Which organ pumps blood around the body?
cards.fact: Your heart beats roughly 100,000 times a day.

cards.prompt: How many chambers does the human heart have?
cards.fact: Two atria receive blood and two ventricles pump it out.

cards.prompt: What is the largest organ of the human body?
cards.fact: An adult's skin covers roughly 1.5 to 2 square meters.

cards.prompt: Which vitamin does your skin make when exposed to sunlight?
cards.fact: Ultraviolet-B light triggers vitamin D production in the skin.

cards.prompt: Which blood type is known as the universal red-cell donor?
cards.fact: O negative red cells can be given to almost anyone in an emergency.

cards.prompt: Which organ produces insulin?
cards.fact: Frederick Banting and Charles Best discovered insulin in 1921.

cards.prompt: Which part of the brain is mainly responsible for balance and coordination?
cards.fact: Cerebellum means "little brain," yet it holds more than half of the brain's neurons.

cards.prompt: Which protein carries oxygen in red blood cells?
cards.fact: The iron in hemoglobin is what makes blood red.

cards.prompt: What is the hardest substance in the human body?
cards.fact: Enamel cannot grow back once it is lost, because it contains no living cells.
